name: Graph Traversal: BFS and DFS
intent: Know when to reach for breadth-first and when for depth-first search, what the visited set is for, how their memory differs (wide against deep), why recursion can crash on a long chain, and why only BFS gives the fewest-hops path.
scenario: A tool follows dependencies, links or moves through a graph with 10,000 nodes. The recursive version works on the test graph and dies with a stack overflow on a chain of 10,000 nodes. The queue-based version is fine on a chain and holds 9,999 nodes at once on a star. One version returns a path of 9,900 edges between two corners of a grid where 198 would do, and a version without a visited set never finishes.
problem: Breadth-first and depth-first search both visit every reachable node and check every edge, so their running time looks the same on paper. They differ in what they remember (a wide frontier or a deep path), in the order they find things, and in which questions they can answer. Pick the wrong one and you get a crash from depth, memory blow-up from width, or a plausible path that is not the shortest. Forget the visited set and even a small graph can cost exponentially many steps or never end.

howItWorks.title: Same graph, different waiting list
howItWorks.text: Both searches keep a list of nodes found but not yet explored. Breadth-first search takes from the front of a queue, so it explores in rings: first the start, then everything one edge away, then two edges away. Depth-first search takes from the top of a stack (or the call stack, when written recursively), so it follows one path as far as it goes and only then backs up. With a visited set both do work proportional to nodes plus edges: for a 10,000-node grid, 39,600 edge checks each. That equal cost is why the choice rests on memory and on what you need to find.

howItWorks.title: The visited set is the algorithm
howItWorks.text: Mark a node when you first see it, and never put a marked node on the list again. Without it, an undirected graph sends the search back along the edge it just used, forever: on small graphs of 100 nodes the model gave up at 100,000 steps for a chain, a tree and a grid alike. Even without any cycle the work can explode, because each node is reached by every path to it: a chain of 20 diamonds (41 nodes) costs 2,097,151 node entries without a visited set and 41 with one. For breadth-first search, mark when you enqueue, not when you dequeue: otherwise one node can sit in the queue many times.

howItWorks.title: Memory follows the shape: wide or deep
howItWorks.text: BFS holds the frontier, the nodes one ring out, so its queue is largest on a wide graph: 9,999 nodes on a 10,000-node star and 5,000 on a binary tree, but only 1 on a chain. DFS holds the current path, so its depth is largest on a long thin graph: 10,000 frames on a chain or a grid and 14 on the binary tree. A recursive DFS needs one call frame for each step of that depth, and runtimes limit it (Python's default is 1,000 frames, and other runtimes have stack-size limits of their own), so a graph that is too deep crashes the recursive version. Rewrite it with your own stack, which only needs heap memory, when depth can be large.

howItWorks.title: What each one is for
howItWorks.text: BFS finds the path with the fewest edges in an unweighted graph, because it finishes every node at distance d before any at distance d + 1: 198 edges to the far corner of the grid. DFS finds some path, usually a long one (9,900 edges there), but its depth-first order is what you want for cycle detection, topological ordering, finding connected components, backtracking through choices, and exploring a tree or a state space where the answer lies deep. Both can be used to count components or test reachability. Once edges have different costs, fewest edges is no longer the cheapest path, and the next concept takes over.

howItWorks.title: Two flavours of DFS give different orders
howItWorks.text: A recursive DFS enters the first neighbour, goes all the way down, and only then tries the second. The common iterative version pushes every neighbour at once and pops the last one first, so it visits neighbours in reverse order, and its stack can hold the same node more than once (9,802 entries on the 10,000-node grid, close to the recursive depth). Both are valid depth-first searches with the same cost on paper. If you need the same visiting order as the recursive one, keep an explicit stack of a node and the index of its next neighbour, the way the code samples do.

pros: Both enter each node once and check each edge once per end: work proportional to nodes plus edges
BFS gives the fewest-edges path in an unweighted graph
DFS uses memory proportional to the depth of the path, small on a wide, shallow graph
Both work on implicit graphs (grids, puzzle states, dependency lists) that are never stored
cons: BFS needs memory for a whole frontier, which can be most of the graph
Recursive DFS can overflow the stack on deep graphs, and the limit is a property of the runtime
DFS paths are not shortest paths
Neither handles edge weights: for cheapest paths you need Dijkstra or similar
whenToUse: BFS: fewest hops (social distance, minimum moves in a puzzle, network hops), level-by-level processing, nearest match
DFS: cycle detection, topological sort, connected components, backtracking and exhaustive search of choices
Either: reachability, 'is everything connected', collecting every node from a start
whenNotToUse: Weighted edges where cost matters: use Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford or A*
BFS on a very wide graph or state space where the frontier will not fit in memory
Recursive DFS on input depth you do not control, unless you have set a limit and a fallback
A question an index already answers, such as a direct lookup by key: do not build a search for it
pitfalls: No visited set: on an undirected graph the walk goes back and forth along an edge and never ends (gave up at 100,000 steps in the model), and on a chain of 20 diamonds it costs 2,097,151 node entries instead of 41
Marking visited when dequeuing instead of enqueuing in BFS: a node reachable from several queued nodes is queued several times, so the queue and the work grow beyond the number of nodes

Recursive DFS on a deep graph: a chain or a snake-shaped grid of 10,000 nodes needs a depth of 10,000 frames, past Python's default limit of 1,000; raising the limit only helps while the real thread stack holds out, and past that the process can crash instead of raising an error
Using DFS for 'shortest path': it returned a path of 9,900 edges between two corners of a 10,000-node grid where BFS found 198, and the answer looks fine until someone measures it
Using BFS on a very wide graph and running out of memory: 9,999 of 10,000 nodes were in the queue at once on a star
Forgetting that a graph may be disconnected: one search from one start reaches only its own component, so loop over every unvisited node to cover everything
Assuming the iterative and recursive DFS give the same order: pushing all neighbours reverses their order, so a result that depends on visiting order changes silently when you switch
Using an adjacency matrix on a sparse graph: finding the neighbours of a node costs a pass over a whole row, so the traversal costs about n squared instead of nodes plus edges

roles.label: Caller
roles.description: Asks for reachability, the nearest match or a path.

roles.label: Graph
roles.description: Nodes and edges, stored or generated on demand.

roles.label: Waiting list
roles.description: A queue (BFS) or a stack (DFS) of nodes found but not yet explored.

roles.label: Visited set
roles.description: Remembers which nodes were already found, so none is explored twice.

roles.label: Path
roles.description: The route reported back, shortest only for BFS.

quiz.question: Which graph is most likely to crash a recursive depth-first search with a stack overflow?
options: A star with 10,000 leaves, because the hub has so many neighbours.
A balanced binary tree with 10,000 nodes, because it has many leaves.
Any graph with cycles, because a cycle makes the recursion repeat.
A chain of 10,000 nodes, because the depth equals the number of nodes.
quiz.explanation: Recursion depth is the length of the current path, and a chain makes that path as long as the graph. A star needs depth 2 and a balanced binary tree about 14. With a visited set, cycles do not make the recursion repeat.

quiz.question: Why does breadth-first search find the path with the fewest edges in an unweighted graph?
options: It always chooses the lowest-numbered neighbour, which is the nearest one.
It finishes every node at distance d before any at distance d + 1.
It stores every path it finds and compares their lengths at the end.
It visits fewer nodes than depth-first search on every kind of graph.
quiz.explanation: The queue is first in, first out, so nodes leave it in order of distance from the start. The first time a node is reached, it is reached by the fewest edges. Visiting fewer nodes is not guaranteed: on a grid BFS visited all 10,000 nodes while DFS stopped after 9,901.

quiz.question: A breadth-first search marks a node as visited only when it takes it off the queue, not when it puts it on. What is the main effect?
options: A node reachable from several queued nodes is queued several times, so the queue and the work grow beyond n.
Some nodes are skipped, so parts of the graph are never reached.
The search turns into a depth-first search, because the order of visits is reversed.
Nothing changes in the result or the cost, so the two styles are equivalent.
quiz.explanation: Between being queued and being dequeued a node is still unmarked, so every neighbour that finds it queues it again. The result can still be right, but the queue can grow far past the number of nodes. Marking at enqueue time keeps each node in the queue at most once.
